subChunks.title: SSR Concepts and Next.js Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: Client-side React renders a blank HTML shell, then loads JavaScript, then renders the UI. This is slow for SEO and for users on slow connections. Server-side rendering (SSR) sends fully-rendered HTML from the server — the user sees content immediately, and search engines index it correctly. Next.js is the dominant SSR framework for React, and understanding its rendering models is essential for modern React development.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Rendering models

CSR (Client-Side Rendering): The server sends empty HTML. The browser downloads JS, executes React, renders the UI. Slow initial load, fast subsequent navigation.

SSR (Server-Side Rendering): The server runs React on each request, sends fully rendered HTML. User sees content immediately. React then "hydrates" the HTML (attaches event listeners). Used for pages with per-request data.

SSG (Static Site Generation): Pages are rendered at build time. Served as static HTML — instant, cacheable, CDN-friendly. Used for content that doesn't change per user.

ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration): SSG with time-based revalidation. The static page is served, but regenerated in the background after a specified interval.

Next.js App Router (React Server Components)

// app/quests/page.tsx — Server Component by default:
// No useState, no useEffect, no browser APIs
// Runs on the server, has direct DB access
async function QuestsPage() {
  const quests = await db.query('SELECT * FROM quests'); // Direct DB access!

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Quest Board</h1>
      {quests.map(q => <QuestCard key={q.id} quest={q} />)}
    </main>
  );
}

export default QuestsPage;
// Client Components — opt in with 'use client':
'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';

export function AcceptQuestButton({ questId }) {
  const [pending, setPending] = useState(false);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => { /* client-side logic */ }}>
      {pending ? 'Accepting...' : 'Accept Quest'}
    </button>
  );
}

Server Components vs Client Components

// Server Components can:
// - Access databases, file system, environment variables directly
// - Fetch data without exposing API keys to the client
// - Zero bundle size (they don't ship to the browser)

// Client Components can:
// - Use hooks (useState, useEffect, useReducer, etc.)
// - Use browser APIs (localStorage, window, etc.)
// - Handle user interactions and events

// Rule: server components can import client components
// but client components CANNOT import server components

Data fetching in Next.js App Router

// Fetch in a Server Component — runs on the server:
async function QuestDetail({ params }) {
  // Automatic deduplication — same fetch in multiple components = one request:
  const quest = await fetch(`/api/quests/${params.id}`, {
    next: { revalidate: 60 }, // ISR — revalidate every 60 seconds
  }).then(r => r.json());

  return <div><h1>{quest.title}</h1></div>;
}

// Loading UI with Suspense (streaming):
// app/quests/loading.tsx — shown while QuestsPage loads:
export default function Loading() {
  return <QuestListSkeleton />;
}

When to use each pattern

Vex: "Default to Server Components. Add 'use client' only when you need interactivity or browser APIs. The rule of thumb: leaf components (buttons, inputs, interactive widgets) are client components. Layout components, data fetching components, and pages are server components. Push 'use client' as far down the tree as possible."

// ✅ Push client down — only the interactive part is a client component:
async function QuestPage({ params }) {        // Server Component
  const quest = await fetchQuest(params.id);
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{quest.title}</h1>           {/* Server rendered */}
      <QuestDetails quest={quest} />    {/* Server rendered */}
      <AcceptButton questId={quest.id} /> {/* Client component */}
    </div>
  );
}

storyBeats.text: A search engine crawls the quest board. Blank. No content — just JavaScript. Lighthouse scores the page a 23. Vex pulls up Next.js.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Client-side rendering sends JavaScript first and content second. Server-side rendering sends content first. Next.js App Router takes this further: Server Components run on the server, fetch data directly, ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Only interactive pieces are Client Components.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The mental model: pages and layouts are server-rendered by default. You add 'use client' only when you need hooks or browser APIs. Push that boundary as far down as possible. A page that is 90% server-rendered and 10% client component is faster, lighter, and more SEO-friendly than the reverse.

storyBeats.speaker: Server Component with direct DB access

This is a conceptual exercise (no sandbox for server-side code). Answer these architecture questions:

  • For each component below, decide: Server Component or Client Component?
    - Page that displays a list of quests fetched from a DB
    - A 'Accept Quest' button with onClick handler
    - A layout wrapper that shows navigation
    - A search input wired to useSearchParams
  • Write pseudo-code for the quest detail page showing where you'd split server and client components

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a full Next.js App Router page (in your local environment or a CodeSandbox with Next.js): a quest board at /quests that SSGs the quest list at build time, a quest detail page at /quests/[id] that SSRs per request, and a client component <AcceptQuestButton> that uses useState to show pending state. Write a loading.tsx skeleton for the quest list. Add proper metadata (title, description) using Next.js's Metadata API.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the four rendering models (CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR) — when would you choose each? Then explain the Server Component / Client Component split in Next.js App Router: what can each type do, what is the boundary rule, and what is the performance benefit of maximising Server Components?

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between SSR and SSG in Next.js?
options: SSR renders on every request (dynamic, per-user data); SSG renders once at build time (static, cacheable content)
SSR uses React Server Components; SSG uses traditional React
SSR requires a Node.js server; SSG works on any static host
SSR is faster for the user; SSG is faster for the server
questions.answer: SSR renders on every request (dynamic, per-user data); SSG renders once at build time (static, cacheable content)
questions.explanation: SSR runs the page component on each request — suitable for pages with user-specific data (dashboard, profile). SSG runs at build time — all users get the same pre-built HTML, served from a CDN at near-zero latency. ISR is SSG with automatic background regeneration after a time interval.

questions.prompt: What does adding `'use client'` to the top of a Next.js component file do?
options: Marks the component (and all its imports) as a Client Component — it runs in the browser and can use hooks and browser APIs
Enables client-side caching for the component's data
Tells Next.js to use CSR for this component's route
Disables TypeScript type checking for this file
questions.answer: Marks the component (and all its imports) as a Client Component — it runs in the browser and can use hooks and browser APIs
questions.explanation: 'use client' is a boundary directive — it marks the file and everything it imports as part of the client bundle. The component can use useState, useEffect, and browser APIs. Without it (default), the component is a Server Component: it runs only on the server, can't use hooks, but has direct access to backends and costs zero JS bundle size.

questions.prompt: A Server Component needs to render an interactive 'Accept Quest' button. How do you structure this?
options: Create a separate Client Component file ('use client') for the button, import it into the Server Component, and pass the questId as a prop
Add 'use client' to the top of the Server Component file
Render the button in a useEffect inside the Server Component
Server Components cannot render interactive elements — use a page-level Client Component instead
questions.answer: Create a separate Client Component file ('use client') for the button, import it into the Server Component, and pass the questId as a prop
questions.explanation: Server Components can import and render Client Components — the boundary goes one way (server → client). The Server Component fetches data and renders static content. The AcceptButton Client Component receives questId as a serialisable prop and handles the interaction. This keeps the data-fetching logic on the server while interactive elements live in the client.

questions.prompt: A marketing landing page displays static content that the marketing team updates monthly. Which rendering strategy is most appropriate?
options: SSG with ISR — pre-render at build time for instant delivery, with revalidation every few hours to pick up content updates without a full rebuild
SSR — to ensure the content is always fresh
CSR — marketing pages don't need SEO
SSG without ISR — the team will manually rebuild on each content change
questions.answer: SSG with ISR — pre-render at build time for instant delivery, with revalidation every few hours to pick up content updates without a full rebuild
questions.explanation: A marketing page has static content that changes infrequently. SSG gives instant CDN delivery and perfect Lighthouse scores. ISR adds automatic background regeneration so content updates propagate without a manual rebuild — typically acceptable for monthly-update content with a revalidation window of hours or a day. SSR would add unnecessary server load for content that doesn't change per user.
